unmapped_findings: A-BDP steel composition window (Table 1): 10.0 < X_Mn < 25.0 wt%, 5.0 < X_Al < 12.0 wt%, 0.6 < X_C < 1.0 wt%.
A-BDP steel constituent phases listed in Table 1: α, B2, DO3, γ, κ, β-Mn (the austenite-base duplex phase assemblage of the alloy family).
After aging at 500–800 °C, lath-like ferrite forms along the austenite grain boundaries of A-BDP steels, with B2 phase found within the lath-like ferrite (b0045).

The deformation mechanism of A-BDP steels is strongly affected by the δ-ferrite fraction, the hardness difference between austenite and ferrite, and the ordered phases in ferrite (b0093); austenite generally determines the deformation mechanism when the δ-ferrite fraction is less than 10% (b0094).

In a Fe-27Mn-12Al-0.8C A-BDP steel (27% δ-ferrite fraction), nano κ-carbide also precipitated in austenite under quenching or quenching-ordering annealing conditions, and its size increased with rising ordering annealing temperature; coarse B2 and ultrafine DO3 particles precipitated in ferrite (b0101).

Room-temperature impact energy of A-BDP steels after solution treatment was much higher, even exceeding typical austenite stainless steel, with an obvious ductile-brittle transition below about −100 °C; after aging at 550 °C for 16 h the room-temperature impact energy dropped sharply (e.g. Fe-30Mn-10Al-1C close to 0 J), attributed to κ-carbide precipitation (b0121).
The impact toughness of Fe-Mn-Al-C austenite steels is higher under solution treatment + water quenching than under aging treatment (b0123).

A-BDP microstructure in the quenched state is full austenite; the room-temperature microstructure of single austenite Fe-Mn-Al-C steels is composed of equiaxed austenite together with annealing twins (b0044).
